title: SYSK Selects: How Cremation Works
summary: Selects rerun of the 2010 episode on cremation. Josh introduces it as a rerun chosen for this week. The hosts cover Ralph White's posthumous adventures, cremation history from prehistoric times and China's 8000 BC practice, the Freemasons and French Revolution, and the step-by-step cremation process: pre-cremation checks, removal of pacemakers, implants and mercury fillings, the retort and flame, cremulator grinding, and the 3 to 9 pounds of remains. They discuss cremation furnace construction and fuel, USPS shipping rules for cremated remains, identification tags, and the Tri-State Crematory scandal in Georgia and other crematorium abuse cases. They compare green impacts (carbon emissions, biocremation), religious attitudes toward cremation across Hinduism, Islam, Judaism, Protestants, Catholics, Mormons and Orthodox churches, and cremation rates by country. They also cover what families do with ashes (scattering rules in national parks, ocean scattering distance, memorial reefs, space flights, diamonds, paintings, fireworks), pet cremation, and a few listener emails at the end.

segments.title: Rerun introduction and Ralph White
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects rerun of the August 2010 cremation episode. The hosts banter about Ralph White, a cremated adventurer whose friends scatter small amounts of his ashes on their travels.

segments.title: History of cremation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss cremation's history, which they say dates to prehistoric times, with China practicing it since around 8000 BC. They note Freemasons pushing cremation during the French Revolution in opposition to the Catholic Church, and the Church's long-standing objection tied to resurrection beliefs.

segments.title: Cremation chamber origins and US adoption
segments.summary: The hosts mention the cremation chamber was invented in the late 1800s by Professor Brunetti and began in earnest in the US in Pennsylvania in 1876. They note cremation rates in the US have risen and the reasons people choose it, including land scarcity and burial's environmental impact.

segments.title: Pre-cremation preparation
segments.summary: A coroner examines the body before cremation because it cannot later be exhumed. Pacemakers, silicone breast implants, prostheses and radioactive cancer seeds are removed, while mercury fillings, jewelry and glasses usually remain.

segments.title: The burning process and retort
segments.summary: The body is placed in a cardboard or pine container and slid into a preheated retort at roughly 1,800 degrees Fahrenheit or more. A jet of flame strikes the torso. The hosts describe soft tissue drying, skin blistering, muscles contracting so limbs can move, and bones calcifying before breaking into fragments. Families may watch, and push a button in some Hindu cremations.

segments.title: Cremulator, remains and cremation furnaces
segments.summary: Remaining bone is swept into a cremulator, a grinder that pulverizes it into coarse, gravel-like powder. The process takes two to three hours and yields about three to nine pounds of remains. The hosts discuss furnace construction with specialized firebrick, fuel types (natural gas, propane, diesel, formerly coal), and wet scrubbing of dust.

segments.title: Shipping remains and identification
segments.summary: Cremated remains can be mailed through USPS in a sift-proof box, but UPS and FedEx won't ship them. Remains are tagged, often with a metal disc, and paperwork accompanies the body to avoid mix-ups. The hosts note that small mix-ups can still occur.

segments.title: Crematorium abuse and regulation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Tri-State Crematory scandal in Georgia, where bodies were left in the backyard after the incinerator broke down. Marie Brent Marsh pleaded guilty, and sentences were reduced. They also describe a 2005 Pennsylvania case involving fetal remains, a California case involving selling body parts, and a Mississippi case involving mixed ashes, and note that state regulation varies.

segments.title: Green cremation and religious attitudes
segments.summary: The hosts compare the environmental impact of cremation and burial and cite a 2009 Reuters figure of about 880 pounds of CO2 per cremation. They discuss biocremation (alkaline hydrolysis) and then the views of Hinduism, Sikhism, Jainism, Islam, Judaism, Protestantism, Catholicism, Mormons and Orthodox churches toward cremation.

segments.title: Things families do with ashes
segments.summary: Options include urns, columbaria, scattering and burial. The hosts mention memorials such as ashes in fireworks shot from a cannon, spaceflight by Celestis, synthetic diamonds, ash paintings, and Eternal Reefs memorial reefs. They cite statistics on what families choose, the one percent unclaimed rate, and cremation rates by country.

segments.title: Scattering laws and famous scatterings
segments.summary: The hosts explain that National Park Service leaves scattering to individual parks, that state and national forests are more lax, and that the EPA suggests scattering at sea at least three miles from shore, with California requiring more distance. They recount Steve Goodman's ashes scattered at Wrigley Field and the stolen and burned body of Graham Parsons near Joshua Tree, then mention a scene in The Big Lebowski.

segments.title: Pet cremation and closing
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the growing pet cremation industry, its lack of regulation, and home pet cremation. Josh and Chuck share memories of burying family pets. They then wrap up the cremation episode.

segments.title: Listener mail
segments.summary: Mark from Eastern MD writes about a breakfast sandwich and a Sawnas episode. Katie from Kent, Washington reports her betta fish, Chucker's Junior, jumped out of its bowl.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh asks for listener cremation stories to be sent by email and gives website information.
